officialDocs.label: Release note: 5,000 requests/hour per OAuth token

verdict.summary: Register an OAuth application in the DigitalOcean control panel and any DigitalOcean user can authorize it the same day, with no review, granular resource:action scopes, PKCE and a published authorization-server metadata document. The main gotchas are single-use rotating refresh tokens and that each token is tied to one team.

evidence.label: inferred
evidence.note: Standard authorization-code flow; loopback redirect URIs match any port, which makes local testing easy.

timeToProd.assumes: A confidential web app requesting granular read scopes (and create/update where the agent acts) for the user's selected team.

evidence.label: inferred
evidence.note: The OAuth reference describes registration and use with no review or approval step.

prerequisites.item: A DigitalOcean account that can access the control panel
prerequisites.why: Confidential OAuth applications are registered under Account → API → Applications.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: Whether an account needs a payment method on file before it can register apps wasn't documented.

prerequisites.why: redirect_uri must match a callback URL provided during registration. Loopback URIs (127.0.0.1, [::1], localhost) match on any port.
A refresh token works exactly once and rotates, so concurrent refreshes can lock you out.

scopeTiers.impact: View resources without credentials. kubernetes:read excludes cluster credentials and database:read excludes database credentials.
Create resources, read database credentials, download kubeconfigs or open consoles. Same self-serve path, but a much bigger trust ask on the consent screen.
Read Only or Full Access to the whole API, expanding automatically as endpoints are added.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: Documented for API tokens; that OAuth apps can request these exact aliases is our inference.

scopeTiers.impact: If you omit scope, the consent screen offers 'Manage permissions' so the user picks granular scopes themselves. Your agent must then cope with whatever it gets.

steps.title: Sign in to the control panel
steps.detail: Log in with the account (ideally a company team owner) that should own the OAuth application.

evidence.label: tested
evidence.note: The new-application URL redirected to this login page on 2026-10-20.

steps.title: Register a new OAuth application
steps.detail: Account → API → Applications → Register OAuth Application. Enter name, homepage, description and callback URL.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: Exact form fields beyond the callback URL weren't listed in the reference.

steps.title: Store client ID and secret
steps.detail: Copy both into your secret manager.

steps.title: Pick granular scopes
steps.detail: Map agent actions to resource:action scopes from the scopes reference (for example droplet:read, monitoring:read, app:read) and avoid credential scopes unless needed.

steps.title: Implement authorize with PKCE
steps.detail: Redirect to https://cloud.digitalocean.com/v1/oauth/authorize with client_id, redirect_uri, response_type=code, scope, state and an S256 code_challenge.

evidence.label: tested
evidence.note: S256 and the endpoints appear in the live authorization-server metadata.

steps.title: Implement token exchange and rotation
steps.detail: POST to https://cloud.digitalocean.com/v1/oauth/token with grant_type=authorization_code (client_secret_post). Save access_token, refresh_token and info.team_uuid. Refresh with grant_type=refresh_token and replace both tokens atomically.

steps.title: Call the API
steps.detail: Use Authorization: Bearer <token> against https://api.digitalocean.com/v2 (for example GET /v2/droplets). Remember each token acts on one team.

steps.title: Test with another account and team
steps.detail: Authorize from a different DigitalOcean account and team; check the consent screen and that team_name matches what the user picked.

agentCanDo: Write the PKCE authorize, callback and refresh code
Register public clients via the dynamic registration endpoint
Read the authorization-server metadata to configure the client
humanMustDo: Sign in and register the confidential OAuth application
Test consent from a second account and team

blockers.symptom: Token endpoint returns {"error":"invalid_request","error_description":"The provided authorization grant is invalid, expired, revoked, does not match the redirection URI used in the authorization request, or was issued to another client."}
blockers.cause: Bad or reused code, or redirect_uri differing from the authorize request.
blockers.fix: Send the identical redirect_uri and exchange each code once.

blockers.symptom: Refresh fails with invalid grant and the user has to reconnect
blockers.cause: A refresh token can be used exactly once; two workers refreshing at the same time leaves one with a dead token, and using it invalidates the old access token.
blockers.fix: Serialize refreshes per connection with a lock and persist the new pair before using it.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: The exact error body on a reused refresh token wasn't documented.

blockers.symptom: Agent can't see the user's other projects or droplets
blockers.cause: The token is issued for one team (info.team_uuid/team_name in the token response).
blockers.fix: Let the user connect once per team and store tokens per team_uuid.

evidence.label: inferred
evidence.note: The reference shows team info per token but doesn't explicitly say tokens are limited to one team.

blockers.symptom: 403 on some endpoints despite a successful connect
blockers.cause: The user unticked scopes in 'Manage permissions', or you omitted scope and they chose a narrow set.
blockers.fix: Check the scope field in the token response and degrade gracefully or ask for reconsent.

blockers.cause: The API is limited to 5,000 requests per hour per OAuth token.
blockers.fix: Cache, paginate efficiently, and back off on 429.

evidence.label: sourced
evidence.note: Release note last verified 2021; a per-minute limit may also apply.

nuances.text: Access tokens last 30 days for confidential clients and one hour for public clients. Refresh tokens are single-use and rotate.
Public clients (CLIs, desktop apps, MCP servers) can self-register with POST https://cloud.digitalocean.com/v1/oauth/register and get a client_id without a secret; up to five redirect URIs.
DigitalOcean publishes RFC 8414 metadata at /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server with PKCE S256 and a registration endpoint, which suits MCP-style agent clients.

evidence.label: tested
evidence.note: Fetched live on 2026-10-20; client_id_metadata_document_supported is false.

nuances.text: Revoke tokens with https://cloud.digitalocean.com/v1/oauth/revoke when a user disconnects.
Granular scopes separate viewing a resource from viewing its credentials (for example database:read vs database:view_credentials), so an agent can inspect infrastructure without holding secrets.

sources.title: DigitalOcean release note: rate limit per OAuth token raised to 5,000/hour

tested: GET https://cloud.digitalocean.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server: issuer https://cloud.digitalocean.com, authorize/token/register/revoke endpoints, PKCE S256, auth methods client_secret_post and none
POST https://cloud.digitalocean.com/v1/oauth/token with dummy values: invalid_request 'The provided authorization grant is invalid...'
openQuestions: Whether OAuth apps can request api:read / api:write aliases, or only granular scopes
Whether a token can ever span more than one team
Current per-minute rate limit for OAuth tokens (only the 5,000/hour note was found)
Whether an account must have a verified payment method to register an OAuth app
Whether DigitalOcean restricts or reviews apps with many users
